title: EDUCATION | 5.25.26 Why the 'Conceptual Understanding' Debate Is Arguing Over the Wrong Premise
author: Brendan
summary: The debate between procedural fluency and conceptual understanding has stalled because neither side has a precise vocabulary for what a concept actually is. Drawing on Tiemann and Markle's taxonomy, the article defines a concept as a mental category with Critical Attributes (must-haves) and Variable Attributes (can-haves): concept learning has occurred only when a student can correctly classify a completely novel, unseen instance. This framework clarifies the most common instructional error—the proceduralization of concepts—which occurs when a concept-teaching tool like a bar model is turned into a mandatory drawing algorithm, teaching a new procedure rather than the underlying category. It also clarifies valid concept assessment: tests that ask students to respond to new instances, not reproduce familiar diagrams. The Instructional Hierarchy of Haring and Eaton provides the developmental sequence: concept acquisition must precede fluency, which precedes generalization; collapsing these stages produces the problems both sides of the debate diagnose. Procedural and conceptual understanding are genuinely different cognitive architectures requiring different instructional designs, and the Tiemann-Markle framework makes both teachable and assessable with precision.
points: * A concept is a mental category defined by Critical Attributes (must-haves) and Variable Attributes (can-haves); concept learning occurs only when a student classifies novel, unseen instances correctly. * Proceduralizing concepts—turning a concept-teaching tool into a mandatory step-by-step routine—teaches a new procedure, not the underlying category. * Valid concept assessment asks students to respond to new instances, not define or reproduce familiar diagrams; the latter tests only memorized verbal algorithms. * Procedural fluency and conceptual understanding are different cognitive architectures requiring different instructional designs—conflating them is the source of most classroom confusion in this debate. * The Instructional Hierarchy requires acquisition to precede fluency, which precedes generalization—collapsing these stages produces exactly the problems both sides of the debate are trying to solve.
quotes: A concept is a mental category, a class of objects, symbols or events that share common, defining characteristics. Concept learning has occurred when a student can look at a completely novel, unseen instance and correctly identify whether it belongs in that category or not based on its attributes.
The common error in progressive pedagogy is trying to teach a concept by turning the explanation into a mandatory, step-by-step procedure. I call this the 'proceduralisation' of concepts.

If you force a student to draw a specific bar model, a rectangle or a fraction wall every single time they solve a problem, you have not taught the concept. You have simply taught a drawing algorithm.

We do not test a concept by asking students to define the concept or to reproduce a familiar diagram they saw on the whiteboard. Those are simply verbal or motor algorithms that can be memorised and regurgitated on cue.
Procedural fluency and conceptual understanding are different cognitive architectures. Both matter. Both require instructional designs built for their specific demands.

If the term 'understanding' continues to blur our thinking, we can set it aside and speak directly about concepts, procedures and the behaviours that demonstrate each. Once we do, the debate becomes far less mysterious and the path to better teaching becomes far easier to see.
